evidence.summary: Four things, if I'm honest about what this month actually was. The day on the ridge when the cloud came down and I stood on wet rock for an hour not knowing which way was down, and then the view opened and I have never seen anything like it; I still don't know whether to call that day good or bad, and I've stopped trying. The afternoon the van hit the car with my nephew in the back seat, and the three hours waiting while they checked him over, and the plain fact that it happened on my watch. Then the email that said I hadn't passed, two marks short, and having to walk into an office full of people who knew I'd sat it and say nothing. And my sister turning up at the door with a bag of oranges and a drawing of a fire engine, and four hours of talking, and the feeling of my shoulders finally coming down from around my ears. Everything else this month was weather. Those four were the month.

This month had a hundred days in it, and a wedding where I sat with sparkling water and a slice of lime and for the first time didn't explain myself to anyone; I woke the next morning with steady hands and knew something had turned. Three days later my partner packed a bag and went to their brother's for "a pause", and I wrote down exactly what they said so I wouldn't rewrite it, and I didn't text. Then the resit result, twelve marks over, read on the stairs, shouted down the phone to my sister, the first thing in a long time I could say I'd earned outright. And at the end of the month, in a pharmacy queue of all places, the friend I'd disappeared on five years ago said my name, and I sat with her for an hour and finally told her the truth, and walked home carrying relief and shame at the same time and not knowing which was heavier. A hundred days, a bag by the door, an email, a queue. That was the month.

Three days alone on the hills at the start of the month, nearly cancelled, a knot in my stomach the whole first night in the hostel and then, on the second morning, gone; I cried on the summit and didn't mind, and I came down knowing I could be on my own and be all right. A week later the conversation with my partner that ended it, by agreement, in our own kitchen, and I was the one who said it, and everything since dates from that afternoon. Then the director in the small room with the broken blind offering me the lead, and me saying yes without hedging, and trying for once to let good news be as big as it actually is instead of folding it away. And the next evening my old friend at my table, a bottle of elderflower, photos from the old flat with a colander on my head, the kind of hug where you lean. Grief, pride, a chair, a mended thing. That's what mattered this month.

What mattered this month, if I am honest about it, comes down to four things. My sister told me she is moving overseas in the autumn, and I sat on the kitchen floor afterwards being proud and gutted at the same time; I still have not decided which one is winning. Then a year without a drink, marked with a walk, a plate of dumplings and an early night, which is exactly how I wanted it marked. The day after that, the exam result: third attempt, the one word, read twice in a stairwell before I rang my mother. And then dinner at my parents' place, when Dad stopped breathing over his steak and I was the one who got up and did something about it. He is fine. He is making jokes about it in the family chat. I keep listing those last three together because they landed within a few days of each other and I have not caught up with any of them yet. It was a loud month, mostly in good ways, with one long goodbye started and a clearer sense of what I am able to do when it counts.

This month started with the barrier. The car spun on the ring road and hit it twice, and I walked away with nothing broken and a week of seeing the second hit every time I closed my eyes. I am still not entirely back behind the wheel, in any sense. Then, in the middle of the month, the restaurant: my partner's reaction, the injector, the ambulance, her hand in mine saying my name, and the slow day at home afterwards, which was somehow one of the best we have had. Late in the month my oldest friend told me the group had been meeting without me for most of a year, and that she had organized it. I paid for the drinks and walked for an hour. I do not know yet what is left of that circle. And two days later I finished the marathon, nearly an hour off the plan, walking the last six miles beside a stranger in a frog hat, prouder of the walking than of the running. A month of near misses and real hits, and I am still working out which was which.
